result: The study analyzed 10,036 UpToDate articles sampled quarterly from 2011-2020, capturing 169,203 unique versions and extracting 83,423 unique references from 4,055 journals. These 37,050 newly cited articles from 887 specialty journals were compared against 2.4 million uncited articles published in the same journals during the same period.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C63-C66 provide consistent, explicit descriptions of the dataset composition with specific numbers that align across abstract, results, and methods sections. The sampling methodology using WayBackMachine is clearly described, and the numbers are internally consistent (e.g., 83,423 total references filtered to 37,050 from specialty journals).

result: Citation rates in UpToDate varied substantially across 18 medical specialties, ranging from 0.4% (pathology) to 2.4% (neurology). The highest rates were in neurology (2.4%), rheumatology (2.3%), hematology (2.3%), and pediatrics (2.2%), while the lowest were in pathology (0.4%), geriatrics (0.6%), and radiology (0.7%).
evaluation: Claims C4 and C16-C22 provide explicit numerical data with specific citation rates and article counts for each specialty. The data is internally consistent and clearly presented with both percentages and absolute numbers, allowing verification of the calculations.

result: Clinical trial citation rates were highly variable across specialties. In 9 of 18 specialties, less than 10% of phase III clinical trials were cited. Practice guidelines had the highest citation rate (>13% in 9 specialties), while no equivalence trials (0 of 43 published) were ever cited. Internal medicine showed the highest clinical trial citation rate at 36.3%.
evaluation: Claims C5, C23-C25, and C70-C72 provide explicit data on clinical trial citation patterns with specific percentages and counts. The finding that no equivalence trials were cited is particularly striking and well-documented. The variation across specialties is clearly quantified.

result: Pragmatic clinical trials were cited in only 5 of 18 specialties, with oncology citing 50%, internal medicine 20.3%, endocrinology 11.1%, cardiology 8.0%, and pediatrics 7.7%. The remaining 13 specialties had 0% citation rates for pragmatic trials.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 and C73-C77 provide explicit percentages for pragmatic trial citations across specialties. The data clearly shows limited adoption of this trial type, with specific quantification for each specialty that cited them.

result: Case reports represented one of the three most commonly cited article types in 12 of 18 specialties, despite only 0.8% (3,111 of 403,043) of published case reports being cited overall. In dermatology, case reports comprised 32.0% of citations, and in pathology 15.5%. By comparison, phase III clinical trials represented less than 1.0% of added citations in 9 of 18 specialties. Oncology was unique in having phase III trials among the most cited types (411 of 3,071 references).
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C28-C33, and C79 provide detailed quantification of case report citation patterns with specific percentages and counts. The contrast between low overall citation rates but high representation among cited articles is clearly documented. The data for specific specialties like dermatology and oncology is explicitly stated.

result: Six specialties (anesthesiology, cardiology, critical care, geriatrics, internal medicine, and oncology) favored higher-quality evidence, with reviews/systematic reviews, practice guidelines, and meta-analyses representing the three most cited article types in five of these six specialties.
evaluation: Claims C8 and C78 explicitly identify specialties favoring higher-quality evidence and specify the article types most commonly cited. The data is clearly presented and references Figure 1 for visual support.

result: Time-to-citation varied by article type but not by specialty. Overall, 50% of articles were cited within one year (IQR 0-4 years). Phase III clinical trials had the shortest time-to-citation (75% within one year, IQR 0-1 year), while case reports had the longest (median 3 years, IQR 1-9 years). Higher quality evidence correlated with shorter time-to-citation across all specialties.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C80 provide explicit time-to-citation statistics with medians and IQRs. The correlation between evidence quality and citation speed is clearly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

result: Journal impact factor was significantly correlated with citation proportion in 12 of 18 specialties, with correlations ranging from rho=0.86 (p=1.4×10⁻⁶) in rheumatology to rho=0.29 (p=0.01) in oncology. The remaining six specialties showed no significant relationship (p>0.05).
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 and C81-C89 provide explicit statistical correlations with Spearman's rho values and p-values for each specialty. The statistical tests are appropriate for the data type, and the results are clearly presented with specific values for each specialty.

result: Journal impact factor was significantly and negatively correlated with time-to-citation in 10 of 18 specialties, indicating that articles from higher impact journals were cited more quickly. Correlations ranged from rho=-0.51 (p=0.03) in infectious diseases to rho=-0.31 (p=0.006) in oncology.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 and C90-C99 provide explicit negative correlations with statistical significance values. The interpretation that higher impact journals lead to quicker citation is clearly stated and supported by the data. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provides visual support.

result: Abstract contents, assessed using UMLS concepts, can significantly explain both whether articles are cited in point-of-care resources and variation in time-to-citation among cited abstracts.
evaluation: Claim C45 is explicitly stated and supported by Figures 3 and 3—figure supplements 1-4, which show word clouds of over- and under-represented concepts. The use of SciSpacy for UMLS extraction is described in the methods (C67).

result: Average annual department-specific NIH funding correlated strongly with the absolute number of citations across all specialties, with correlations ranging from rho=0.73 (p=1.2×10⁻¹⁰) in pathology to rho=0.41 (p=0.006) in infectious diseases. Ten specialties showed significant correlations.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 and C100-C106 provide explicit correlations between NIH funding and citation counts with statistical significance. The data is clearly presented with specific rho and p-values for each specialty, and Figures 4 and 5 provide visual support.

result: NIH funding did not correlate with time-to-citation in any specialty, contrasting sharply with its strong correlation with absolute citation numbers.
evaluation: Claim C50 explicitly states the lack of correlation between NIH funding and time-to-citation, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1. This finding is clearly distinguished from the funding-citation number relationship.

result: Using linear modeling of NIH funding versus citations, the estimated cost per new UpToDate citation ranged from $874.85 (pathology) to $48,086.18 (urology/nephrology), with intermediate costs for other specialties. The model was not significant for infectious diseases.
evaluation: Claims C9 and C51-C59 provide specific cost estimates with standard errors and intercepts. However, the linear modeling approach has significant limitations: (1) the model assumes a causal relationship from correlation data, (2) confounding factors are not addressed (e.g., other funding sources, institutional factors, specialty-specific publication patterns), (3) the intercept interpretation as 'set-up cost' is not validated, (4) the model does not account for time lags between funding and publication/citation, and (5) city-level aggregation may introduce ecological fallacy. While the correlations are strong, the causal interpretation and cost estimates require additional validation.

result: The analysis focused on the United States because 35% of UpToDate citations were from US sources (compared to 39% of all PubMed publications in 2019). Eight specialties were combined under 'general and internal medicine' for NIH funding analysis due to overlapping departmental funding structures.
evaluation: Claims C108-C109 and C113 provide explicit justification for the US focus and methodological decisions about specialty grouping. The percentages are clearly stated and the rationale for combining specialties is explained.

result: Approximately 18% of articles had no primary affiliation listed.
evaluation: Claim C114 is explicitly stated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 caption. This represents a limitation in the geographic analysis but is clearly documented.

result: Preliminary analysis revealed that some specialties (e.g., cardiology and oncology) demonstrated clear bias toward particular disease topics and treatment paradigms, while others (e.g., endocrinology and metabolism) were more diverse in topic coverage.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are explicitly stated in the discussion with specific examples. The authors acknowledge this is preliminary and warrants further investigation, appropriately qualifying the strength of the conclusion.

result: The low citation rates, particularly for clinical trials and practice guidelines designed to address clinical uncertainty, suggest a translational block between research publication and clinical practice. NIH funding patterns may partially dictate which research successfully reaches point-of-care, though inadequate study design may also contribute to low citation rates.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C117-C119 represent interpretations and speculations about causality. While the low citation rates are well-documented, the attribution to 'translational block' versus other factors (study quality, clinical relevance, alternative dissemination channels) is not definitively established. The discussion appropriately acknowledges multiple possible explanations, but the causal claims remain speculative.

result: The study is motivated by healthcare system underperformance due to patients not receiving recommended services and receiving unnecessary treatments. The challenge is the absence of evidence to assess treatment appropriateness. UpToDate serves as a reliable, widely-used point-of-care resource with quantifiable impact on patient care, making it suitable for studying clinical research translation.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15, C62, C110-C111 cite appropriate sources for background claims about healthcare system problems and UpToDate's characteristics. The citations support the rationale for using UpToDate as a proxy for clinical research translation, though limitations are acknowledged.

result: The study used SciSpacy to extract UMLS concepts from abstracts and the WayBackMachine to archive UpToDate articles over time.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C112 describe methodological tools with appropriate citations. The use of established tools (SciSpacy, WayBackMachine) is clearly documented.

result: The study acknowledges several limitations: alternative information sources exist but are too informal for systematic analysis; UpToDate relevance varies by specialty and training; citation does not necessarily indicate practice changes; and specialty divisions using journal classifications do not fully capture overlap between fields.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 explicitly acknowledge study limitations in the discussion section. These are appropriate caveats that strengthen the interpretation of results by clearly stating what the study does and does not demonstrate.

result: The study concludes that successful specialties demonstrate translational strategies that should be applied more broadly. The dataset and methods are designed to generate hypotheses about research translation and provide a baseline for monitoring research investment efficiency.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 represent the study's stated goals and conclusions. These are appropriately framed as descriptive/exploratory findings that generate hypotheses rather than definitive causal conclusions. The authors clearly state the intended purpose of the work.
